Long-term biogas desulfurization under different microaerobic conditions in
full-scale thermophilic digesters co-digesting high-solid sewage sludge
Andrea Giordanoa, Francesco Di Capuab,∗, Giovanni Espositob, Francesco Pirozzib
a Acqua & Sole s.r.l., Via Giulio Natta, Vellezzo, Bellini, PV, Italy
b Department of Civil, Architectural and Environmental Engineering, University of Naples Federico II, via Claudio 21, 80125, Naples, Italy
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Biogas desulfurization
Microaeration
Thermophilic digestion
Full-scale digesters
Sulfide removal
A B S T R A C T
Long-term (81 weeks) microaerobic biogas desulfurization was investigated in three full-scale thermophilic
digesters in series co-digesting sewage sludge with co-products of source segregated domestic food waste.
Residual oxygen (RO) concentrations in the digester headspaces were maintained at fixed values from 2.0% to
0.2% (v/v). Complete H2S removal was obtained at all tested RO concentrations under organic loading rate
(OLR) and hydraulic retention time (HRT) varying between 1.5 and 2.3 kg VS/m3 d and between 44 and 71 d,
respectively. Specific oxygen and air consumptions of 0.88 kg O2/ton VSin and 0.73 %ton air/ton biogas, re-
spectively, were obtained by linear regressions with the RO values maintained in the biogas. Mass balance and
stoichiometric evaluations revealed that from 13% to 59% of the consumed O2 was used for processes other than

1. Introduction
Anaerobic digestion (AD) is widely used for the treatment of organic
waste such as agro-waste, sewage sludge and the organic fraction of
municipal solid waste. During this process, almost 95% of the organic
matter and 90% of the energy that originally exist in the substrate are
retained as biogas (Guerrero et al., 2015). The biogas produced from
the digestion of sewage sludge typically contains 55–65% of CH4,
35–44% of CO2 and small concentrations of other gases (Rasi et al.,
2011). Hydrogen sulfide (H2S) commonly occurs in biogas due to the
anaerobic fermentation of sulfur-containing organic molecules (i.e.
proteins) and the activity of sulfate-reducing bacteria (SRB) coupling
the oxidation of organics and hydrogen gas (H2) to the complete re-
duction of sulfate (SO4
2−) and other oxidized sulfur compounds
(Abatzoglou and Boivin, 2009; Papirio et al., 2013a, 2013b). The con-
centration of H2S in biogas varies from a few hundred to ten thousand
ppm depending on the amount of bioavailable sulfur compounds in the
feedstock and the outcome of the competition among SRB, acetogens
and methanogens for the organic substrates (Stams et al., 2005).
Elevated concentrations of H2S have detrimental effects on biogas
equipment and significantly reduce the economic value and reuse po-
tential of biogas (Khanongnuch et al., 2018). H2S conversion to sulfur
oxides (SOx) and sulfuric acid (H2SO4) during biogas combustion results
in severe corrosion of the piping system and other industrial installa-
tions. H2S levels in biogas should not exceed 1000 ppm if traditional
boilers and internal combustion engines are utilized for electricity
generation and even stricter limits (< 0.1 ppm) are required for off-site
biogas utilization, e.g. as vehicle fuel or in fuel cells (Rasi et al., 2011).
H2S and SOx are also responsible for poisoning and deactivation of the
oxidation catalysts applied for biogas valorization (Mancino et al.,
2016; Ortloff et al., 2016). Additionally, free H2S levels above 50 mg/L
can severely inhibit methanogenic activity (Oude Elferink et al., 1994).
Microaeration has been reported as an efficient and cost-effective
method for in-situ H2S removal from biogas (Krayzelova et al., 2014).
This method consists in delivering a limited flux of air to the digester
headspace in order to trigger the biological oxidation of the H2S con-
tained in the biogas, which is carried out by mats of sulfur-oxidizing
bacteria forming on the internal walls of the headspace and on the li-
quid surface (Kobayashi et al., 2012). As shown by Eqs. (1) and (2)
(Tilahun et al., 2018), microaerobic H2S oxidation results in the pro-
duction of SO4
2−and biogenic S0, the latter forming white deposits in
the digester headspace which could be recovered and reused for water
and wastewater treatment (Di Capua et al., 2019, 2016).

Microaerobic conditions require a small oxygen supply, which re-
sults in limited cost and energy consumption for aeration. The potential
drawbacks of microaeration include (1) methane dilution (especially if
air is used instead of pure oxygen), (2) clogging of gas pipes due to S0
accumulation and (3) inhibition of methanogenesis, although no sig-
nificant oxygen inhibition on methanogenic activity was observed in
previous studies (Krayzelova et al., 2015). As a result, optimization of
oxygen/air dosing to the digester is necessary to maintain high quality
standards for biogas production, reduce maintenance and operational
costs and meet the requirements of biogas utilization technologies (Awe
et al., 2017).
Full-scale anaerobic digesters require an even more accurate control
of microaeration to avoid lack or surplus of oxygen in biogas due to
fluctuations in feedstock composition and H2S production. Different
strategies have been proposed to control microaerobic biogas de-
sulfurization. The oxidation reduction potential (ORP) was reported as
a suitable parameter to control oxygen/air dosing when maintained at
values between −310 and −230 mV (Khanal et al., 2003; Nghiem
et al., 2014). In contrast, Diaz et al. (2010) observed that the re-
lationship between ORP and micro-oxygenation was not significant
and, therefore, oxygen dosing control based on ORP response was not
reliable. Ramos and Fdz-Polanco (2014) proposed biogas production as
a control parameter under steady sulfur loadings, whereas H2S con-
centration in biogas was suggested as a suitable regulating parameter
under variable sulfur loadings. However, the use of these two para-
meters for full-scale operation may result in technical and operational
issues: (1) biogas production would be overestimated in case of com-
parable air and biogas flows, inducing an increase of air dosage that
may disrupt the anaerobic process (Krayzelova et al., 2015); (2) a
correct measurement of biogas production usually requires the in-
stallation of a biogas flow meter on long straight pipes for each digester
(EN ISO 5167-2). A full-scale implementation of this configuration with
multiple digesters is challenging; (3) online electrochemical sensors
monitoring H2S levels in the digester headspace commonly experience a
loss of analytical sensitivity due to S0 deposition on the electrodes (Hall
and Schoenfisch, 2018; Pandey et al., 2012). As a result, air dosing
control based on H2S measurement might not be reliable for long-term
operation.
Previous studies focused on the effect of microaeration on meso-
philic digestion especially at pilot (Diaz et al., 2011; Ramos et al.,
2014b) and full scale (Jeníček et al., 2017, 2008). In this study, the
desulfurization performance of three full-scale thermophilic digesters in
series was monitored for 81 weeks under different microaerobic re-
gimes. The impact of the different microaerobic conditions on ther-
mophilic biogas production was also evaluated.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Full-scale plant description
The full-scale plant is located near Pavia (Italy) and consists of three
thermophilic digesters (D1, D2 and D3) in series (Fig. 1) treating up to
120 kton/year of high-solid (about 18.5%) organic waste. Each digester
has total and headspace volumes of approximately 4500 m3 and less
than 500 m3, respectively. A direct injection of saturated steam
(p = 4 bar) and insulation by a 10 cm polystyrene layer on the external
wall maintain the digestate at 55 °C and the headspace at 45–50 °C in
winter and 50–55 °C in summer. The feedstock is first collected in ba-
sins and then moved to a mixing unit to be heated and homogenized
with the digestate from D3 and water resulting in a digestate total solid
(TS) and volatile solid (VS) concentrations of 10.7% and 6.6%, re-
spectively. A side-stream ammonia stripping unit is coupled to D1 to
control ammonium concentration in the digestate (Fig. 1). At the end of
the digestion process, the digestate is collected in a 50000 m3 storage
tank prior to being used as fertilizer. The biogas produced by the plant
is converted by a combined heat and power (CHP) system to electrical
energy and primarily consumed on-site (about 30%), while the excess is
sent to the national grid. Biogas treatments, placed upstream the CHP
system, include desulfurization, chilling, condensate removal, com-
pression through blowers and purification with activated carbon filters.
2.2. Operational conditions
During the 81 weeks of the study (from January 2nd, 2017 to July
16th, 2018), the plant treated about 108 kton of feedstock under var-
ious organic loading rate (OLR) and hydraulic retention time (HRT)
conditions (Table 1). The average composition of the feedstock in-
cluded 90% of sewage sludge from municipal and industrial (agrifood
industry) wastewater treatment plants and 10% of co-products (diges-
tate and liquid fraction) of source segregated domestic food waste. H2S
levels ranging between 1200 and 2500 ppm were measured under
completely anaerobic conditions in the biogas produced by a pilot-scale
thermophilic digester fed with the same substrate and operated at OLRs
and HRTs similar to those described in Table 1.
Prior to starting microaeration, the three full-scale digesters were
operated under strict anaerobic conditions (RO < 0.1%) for six
months. Air dosing (kNm3/d) was adjusted manually to maintain the
RO concentrations in the biogas at fixed values in the range of 0.2–2.0%
(v/v) during six different operational periods (P1–P6, Table 1).
2.3. Monitoring and analytical methods
Online biogas production was measured by a ST51 mass flow meter
(FCI, USA) installed as shown in Fig. 1. Biogas composition (CH4, CO2,
H2S and O2) in the three digesters and upstream of the CHP unit was
monitored six times/day using an Optima 7 portable biogas analyzer
(MRU GmbH, Germany). Oxygen dosing to the headspace was per-
formed by using type CL 10/01 (in D1) and CL 4/01 (in D2 and D3) side
channel blowers (Mapro, Italy) and controlled by glass tube flowmeters
(ASA, Italy). Feedstock and digestate samples were periodically col-
lected for VS and TS analyses. Total ammonia nitrogen (TAN) and
carbonate alkalinity (defined as the proton accepting capacity of the
carbonate weak acid subsystem and indicated as H2CO3* alkalinity)
concentrations in the digestate were measured after filtration through
GF3 grade 1.2-μm glass microfiber filters (CHMLAB, Spain). TAN, TS
and VS were measured according to standard methods (APHA, 2005).
H2CO3* alkalinity was measured as described by Lahav et al. (2002).
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Desulfurization performance of the thermophilic digesters
The temporal profiles of RO and H2S concentrations in the biogas
produced by the three thermophilic digesters monitored in this study
are shown in Fig. 2. The desulfurization efficiency was nearly 100% at
all tested RO concentrations as the effluent H2S levels in the biogas
remained below 10 ppm (Table 2). In a previous study, Wu et al. (2016)
studied microaerobic biogas desulfurization at mesophilic (35 °C) and
thermophilic (55 °C) temperatures in a lab-scale fermenter treating rice
straw. O2 was supplied to the fermenter headspace at feed concentra-
tions ranging from 0.5 to 10 times the stoichiometric requirement for
partial H2S oxidation to S0. O2 supply at a 4-fold higher concentration
than the stoichiometric requirement resulted in RO values in biogas
above 0.5% and desulfurization efficiencies of 93.8% and 94.5% under
mesophilic and thermophilic conditions, respectively. O2 supply below
the stoichiometric requirement resulted in RO < 0.25% in biogas and
desulfurization efficiencies below 75%. Similarly, Toth et al. (2015)
observed a significant loss of H2S removal efficiency (25–30%) in a

biotrickling filter treating sulfide-contaminated gas streams when the
RO levels decreased below 1%.
In this study, high-efficiency desulfurization was maintained at RO
concentrations in biogas as low as 0.2% and under OLRs and HRTs
ranging from 1.5 to 2.3 kg VS/m3 d and from 44 to 71 d, respectively
(Table 1). Biogas production ranged between 8.5 and 12.3 ton/d
(Table 2). Nevertheless, linear regressions were obtained between the
RO values maintained in the headspace and both the air-to-biogas ratio
(R2 = 0.94) and specific oxygen supply (R2 = 0.91) (Fig. 3). The in-
tercepts of the two linear regressions on the y axis were 0.73 %ton air/
ton biogas (standard error, SE = 0.17) and 0.88 kg O2/ton VSin
(SE = 0.21) and provide an estimation of the oxygen consumption for
the complete H2S removal in the three digesters per ton of produced
biogas and feed VS, respectively. Slopes were 5.02 (SE = 0.14) and 5.11
(SE = 0.18) for the air-to-biogas ratio and specific oxygen supply re-
gressions, respectively. These values provide a valid support for de-
signing the aeration systems of full-scale thermophilic digesters co-di-
gesting high-solid sewage sludge and optimize oxygen dosing for
desulfurization in order to reduce the aeration costs and improve biogas
quality.
Diaz et al. (2010) supplemented 0.94 and 1.27 Nm3 air/m3 feed to
the headspace of a 200 L mesophilic digester fed with sewage sludge,
corresponding to a specific oxygen supply of approximately 7.9 and
11.9 g O2/kg VSin, respectively. The authors reported that only 30–40%
of the total oxygen supplied to the system served for H2S oxidation,
while the rest left the bioreactor with the produced biogas. This means
that only 2.3–3.5 g O2/kg VSin were used for H2S removal from biogas.
These values are 2.6–4.0 times higher than the specific oxygen con-
sumption observed in our digesters (0.88 g O2/kg VSin) as the H2S
concentration reported by Diaz et al. (2010) in absence of microaera-

dance of SRB in the digester. In a recent study, Han et al. (2019) dosed

(3.5–3.8 g N–NH4
+/kg digestate) were probably higher than those oc-
curring in the mesophilic digester operated by Diaz et al. (2010) as this
was run at a lower solid content (about 1.5% VS). FAN is extremely
toxic to microorganisms and its fraction increases with pH and tem-
perature (Westerholm et al., 2016). As a result, thermophilic operation
results in higher FAN levels compared to mesophilic conditions and can
considerably limit the SRB activity. In this study, the H2S production by
SRB and, thus, S0 accumulation were presumably limited by the high
TAN and FAN levels occurring in the thermophilic digesters. As a result,
thermophilic operation can reduce the costs of digester maintenance
and the frequency of cleaning operations that can disrupt the digestion
process.
A total oxygen consumption of 1.49 L O2/Nm3 biogas was calculated
based on the value of specific air consumption (0.73 %ton air/ton
biogas) estimated in this study. According to Eq. (2), the oxidation of
1200–2500 ppm of H2S to S0 consumes 0.61–1.29 L O2/Nm3 biogas.
This means that, assuming that all H2S oxidized was converted to S0 due
to the limited O2 availability in the headspace, the 13–59% of the
consumed oxygen was not utilized for S0 production. This is in agree-
ment with Ramos et al. (2014a), reporting that between 43% and 55%
of the O2 supplied to the headspaces of two pilot-scale mesophilic di-
gesters was used for processes other than H2S oxidation to S0. It is
possible that the excess O2 was consumed for S0 oxidation to SO4
2−
and/or by facultative/microaerophilic bacteria degrading the organic
substrate as described by Jenicek et al. (2014).
The deposition of S0 onto gas pipes and internal walls of the digester
causes clogging and reduces the biogas storage capacity of the head-
space, resulting in a negative impact on desulfurization efficiency (Diaz
and Fdz-Polanco, 2012). Ramos et al. (2014a) recommended a max-
imum cleaning interval of 14 months to maintain a high O2 usage ef-
ficiency and reduce the cost of microaeration in two pilot-scale diges-
ters with a produced H2S concentration in the biogas of 5000 ppm.
According to Jenicek et al. (2017), strict air dosing into the liquid phase
reduces sulfur deposition and clogging events as less oxygen reaches the
headspace. Although in this work microaeration took place in the
headspace solely, no issues linked to S0 accumulation occurred during
the 81 operational weeks of the study. This can be linked to the limited
H2S production in the digesters due to high TAN levels as well as to
excess oxygen consumption for S0 oxidation to SO4
2−.
3.2. Biogas production and composition under different microaerobic
conditions
Microaeration showed no detrimental effects on thermophilic di-
gestion at the different RO conditions tested. Due to the OLR and HRT
fluctuations (Table 1), the total biogas and CH4 production ranged from
8.5 to 12.3 ton/d and from 3.8 to 6.1 kNm3/d, respectively (Table 2).
The highest specific CH4 production (218 NL/kg VSin) was obtained at a
RO concentration of 0.7% (P4), while a minimum production of 186
NL/kg VSin was observed at RO concentrations of 2.0% (P1) and 0.2%
(P6) (Table 2). CH4 concentration in biogas increased from 56.3% in P1
to 63.4% in P6, whereas CO2 concentration was relatively stable during
the study. This resulted in a 13% increase of the CH4/CO2 ratio in the
produced biogas between P1 (RO = 2.0%) and P6 (RO = 0.2%)
(Table 2). The microaerobic conditions and high TAN levels in the three

digesters likely favored hydrogenotrophic over acetoclastic methano-
genesis, as hydrogenotrophic methanogens possess a higher tolerance
to oxygen (Tang et al., 2004) and ammonia (Angelidaki and Ahring,

In previous studies, microaeration was reported to reduce sulfide
toxicity to methanogens (Jeníček et al., 2008) and enhance hydrolysis
(Johansen and Bakke, 2006; Montalvo et al., 2016) and the aerobic
biodegradation of the volatile fatty acids (VFA) produced during acid-
ogenesis (Jeníček et al., 2014). However, microaeration reduces the
CH4 content of biogas and specific CH4 production due to biogas dilu-
tion and aerobic biodegradation of organic matter, respectively
(Jeníček et al., 2017). In this study, decreasing the RO concentration in
biogas between 2.0% and 0.2% reduced dilution and increased the CH4
content of biogas with no detrimental effects on the H2S removal per-
formance of the three thermophilic digesters (Table 2). CO2 in the
headspace is in equilibrium with bicarbonate alkalinity in the digestate
and depends also on pH and temperature of the liquid phase (Parkin
and Owen, 1986). During the study, CO2 concentration in the biogas
was not expected to vary significantly as both pH and H2CO3* alkalinity
(which can be approximated to bicarbonate alkalinity at the measured
pH values) in the digestate were stable at 7.86
±
0.08 and
9.93 ± 0.91 g CaCO3/L, respectively, as a result of a balanced diges-
tion process.
A 17% increase in the specific CH4 production was observed when
the RO concentration in the digesters was reduced from 2.0% (P1) to
0.7% (P4). The further RO decrease to 0.2% (P6) reduced the specific
CH4 production to the initial value (186 NL/kg VSin, Table 2). Varia-
tions in specific CH4 production can be mainly attributed to fluctuations
in the feedstock composition, which commonly occur during full-scale
plant operation. Additionally, the aerobic substrate biodegradation may
have also influenced CH4 productivity. It is possible that during P1
(RO = 2.0%) more oxygen was available to sustain both hydrolysis and
VFA degradation by facultative bacteria. Decreasing the RO values
below 2.0% likely reduced the aerobic VFA biodegradation and in-
creased CH4 productivity, while RO values below 0.7% may have re-
duced the hydrolytic activity of aerobic bacteria resulting in a lower
specific CH4 production.
3.3. Practical implications and operational remarks
The results of this study show that RO can be reliably used as
control parameter for high-efficiency H2S removal from biogas in full-
scale thermophilic digesters co-digesting sewage sludge. Maintaining
RO concentrations ≥0.2% in biogas resulted in complete desulfuriza-
tion under fluctuating OLR and HRT conditions (Table 1). Single
measurements of RO concentration (as performed in this study) are
preferable to online monitoring especially when H2S levels in biogas are
high in order to avoid sensor poisoning due to long-term exposure.
Biogas upgrading mainly consists in the removal of CO2 and trace
components including H2S, O2 and N2 to meet the standards for bio-
methane production. The European standard EN 16726 sets the CO2, O2
and H2S content in biomethane for pipeline utilization in the range of
2.5–4%, 0.001–1% and ≤5 ppm, respectively. The removal of O2 and
N2 from biogas is expensive and usually performed using membranes or
low-temperature pressure swing adsorption (PSA). As a result, dosing
pure oxygen rather than air is preferable for biomethane production, as
it reduces the post-treatment costs. Our results show that dosing 0.88 kg
of pure oxygen per ton of VSin in the three full-scale thermophilic di-
gesters operated in this study would produce oxygen-free biogas and
reduce the costs of biomethane production. Additionally, the specific
electric consumption during the study was of only 3.4 kWh/ton biogas,
lower than the value of 7.8 kWh/ton biogas calculated based on the
data reported by Diaz et al. (2015) for biogas desulfurization in three
full-scale digesters via microaeration. This confirms microaerobic de-
sulfurization as an inexpensive solution for biogas upgrading.
Introducing air into the headspace of a digester can be considered
safe as far as the RO concentration does not exceed the limiting oxygen
concentration (LOC) of the produced biogas. Dupont and Accorsi
(2006) studied the flammability of biogas mixtures composed of 50%
CH4 and 50% CO2 and determined LOC values of 11.1% and 13.2% for
vapor-saturated and dry biogas, respectively. These values are well
above the RO concentrations (0.2–2.0%) maintained in the three di-
gesters during this study. However, biogas leaks from the digester re-
present a concern and necessary safety measures, especially during
maintenance operations (e.g. cleaning of digesters and biogas storage
tank repair), should be implemented to minimize the risk of explosion.
4. Conclusions
• Complete biogas desulfurization was achieved in three full-scale
thermophilic digesters in series over 81 weeks under various RO
(0.2–2.0%), OLR (1.5–2.3 kg VS/m3 d1) and HRT (44–71 d) condi-
tions.
• The linear relationship between the O2 addition in the headspace
and RO concentration in biogas allowed to estimate a specific
oxygen consumption of 0.88 kg O2/ton VSin (corresponding to
1.49 L O2/Nm3 biogas) for the complete H2S removal from biogas.
• From 13% to 59% of the O2 consumed during the process was not
utilized for H2S conversion to S0.
• The low specific oxygen consumption for H2S removal observed in
this study (1.49 L O2/Nm3 biogas) was presumably due to high TAN
(3.5–3.8 g N–NH4
+/kg digestate) and FAN concentrations in diges-
tate limiting H2S production by SRB.
• No significant S0 accumulation in the headspaces of the three di-
gesters was observed during the study.
• CO2 concentration in the biogas remained stable (32.0–34.3%) at
the different microaerobic conditions investigated, being CO2 in
equilibrium with the pH and bicarbonate alkalinity of the digestate,
which did not vary significantly due to a balanced digestion process.
